text.title: Continuous Discovery Core Rules
text.summary: Seven rules for the weekly discovery cadence and its opportunity-solution tree: the touchpoint floor and who must do it, how opportunities must be phrased and sourced, the single-outcome root, the compare-and-contrast minimum before testing, and the pre-registered threshold every assumption test needs.

rule.statement: `touches` contains at least one customer conversation per ISO week, conducted by a member of the product trio (product, design, engineering) — not relayed by sales, support tickets, or an external research agency. A zero-touch week is recorded as a miss; it is not backfilled by doubling up the following week.

rationale.source: Teresa Torres — Continuous Discovery Habits (2021), definition of continuous discovery

rule.rationale: The definition is weekly touchpoints by the team building the product. Batching four interviews into one month restores the project-based research this practice replaces: decisions taken in the three silent weeks get no customer input, and the batch arrives after they have shipped. Relayed accounts also arrive stripped of the story, leaving only the relayer's interpretation.

rule.statement: `ost_updates` has exactly one target outcome at the root for the cycle, expressed as a product outcome — a customer behaviour the team can move — not a business outcome (revenue, ARR) and not an output (ship feature X).

rationale.source: Torres — Continuous Discovery Habits, outcome chapter

rule.rationale: Two roots make opportunities incomparable, so prioritisation quietly reverts to whoever argues hardest. A revenue root cannot be moved directly by the team's work, so no opportunity under it can ever be shown to have failed, and the tree stops pruning.

rule.statement: Every node in the opportunity space is a customer need, pain or desire in the customer's own words. A node naming a feature, a UI element or a build verb ("add SSO", "redesign the dashboard") is moved into the solution space before the tree is accepted.
rule.rationale: A solution written into the opportunity space pre-commits the branch: everything beneath it explores how to build that specific thing, so the alternative that would have served the same need at a tenth of the cost is never generated. The pre-commitment is invisible afterwards because the tree still looks well-formed.

rule.statement: An opportunity may enter the tree only from a specific past-tense story ("tell me about the last time you…") captured in `signals` with raw_hash + source_url. Opportunities from speculation, from survey free-text, or from a stakeholder request enter marked `unvalidated` and cannot be prioritised until a story backs them.
rule.rationale: Asking what people generally do, or would want, elicits a tidy reconstruction rather than behaviour; asking about one recent instance elicits what actually happened, including the workarounds the customer would never think to mention. Trees built on generalities fill with needs nobody has ever had.

rule.statement: The target opportunity carries at least 3 distinct solutions in the tree before any assumption test is run against it. Testing a single candidate solution is rejected.
rule.rationale: Evaluating one solution asks "is this good enough?", which answers yes almost every time. Comparing three asks "which is best?", and the act of comparing forces the team to state the criteria it was applying implicitly — which is usually where the disagreement was hiding.

rule.statement: Each row in `hypotheses` names the assumption category (desirability, viability, feasibility, usability, ethical), the test, the pass/kill threshold written BEFORE the test ran, and the date. A hypothesis whose status changed without its threshold being crossed is rejected.

rationale.source: Torres — assumption mapping; Bland & Osterwalder — Testing Business Ideas

rule.rationale: Thresholds written after seeing the data migrate to wherever the data landed, so the test can only ever confirm. Pre-registration is the only mechanism that lets a week of discovery actually kill a favoured solution.

rule.statement: Emit a structured skip when the team cannot reach at least one customer or well-qualified prospect per week — pre-launch with no audience, procurement-gated enterprise buyers, a regulated user population with no consent path — or when no single team-controllable outcome exists for the cycle. Route to jtbd-switch-interview as a bounded project instead.

rationale.source: Methodology boundary — continuous cadence vs bounded interview study

rule.rationale: A cadence that misses more weeks than it hits still produces a tree, and the tree keeps its authority while its evidence ages out. Downstream readers cannot see the gap, so stale opportunities get prioritised as if freshly validated.
